listenings.text: Attention, customers. The red line is operating on a detour this weekend because of track work between Belmont and Grand. For the first six months I did the same thing every single time, and it made everything worse. I would walk up to somebody and start with sorry, my English is not very good. And what happens is that people become kind. They slow right down, they speak to you as if you were a child, and the exchange takes three times as long and you understand less at the end of it, not more. Nobody had told me to stop doing that. I worked it out by accident. Two phrases changed everything, and neither of them is difficult. Excuse me, could you tell me. And, when I have not caught it, would you mind repeating that. Four words at the front and you have bought the whole conversation. People stop, they answer properly, and they repeat without deciding anything about you. The other thing took me longer, and it is the blocks. Americans give you distance in blocks, and for a year I was converting blocks into metres in my head while the person was still talking, so I would get the first half of the directions and lose the second. In the end I stopped converting. I just count corners now, like everybody else does.

extra_audio.text: Excuse me, could you tell me where the nearest station is? Would you mind repeating that a little more slowly? Do you know if the train goes downtown from there? Could you tell me how much the fare is? I think I missed my stop. Could you tell me where I should get off? Thank you very much for your help.
